p: - 1–11 · Beginnings: creation, the fall, the flood and Babel. The whole world in a few chapters.
- 12–25 · Abraham: God promises land, descendants and a blessing for all nations.
- 25–36 · Isaac and Jacob: the promise passes down a family full of rivalry.
- 37–50 · Joseph: the family goes down to Egypt, and God turns evil to good.
“This is the account of…”: the same line returns about ten times (2:4, 5:1, 6:9, 10:1, 11:10, 11:27, 25:12, 25:19, 36:1, 37:2), each time narrowing the story toward one family.
The younger first: again and again God’s choice passes over the older son. Isaac over Ishmael, Jacob over Esau, Joseph over his brothers, Ephraim over Manasseh.
Garden to coffin: the book opens with life in Eden and closes with Joseph “in a coffin in Egypt” (50:26), still waiting on the promise.
- 1–7 · Offerings: five kinds of sacrifice, first for the people, then the priests’ side of each.
- 8–10 · Priests: Aaron and his sons are ordained, and Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire.
- 11–15 · Clean and unclean: food, childbirth, skin disease, mildew and the body.
- 16 · The Day of Atonement: the center of the book, once a year, for the whole people.
- 17–27 · Holiness: “Be holy, because I am holy,” worked out in daily life, feasts, Sabbath years and Jubilee.

Why it’s here: the tabernacle is finished at the end of Exodus. Leviticus answers the next question: how can a holy God live among his people? No one travels in this book; it all happens at the foot of Sinai.
“Love your neighbor as yourself” first appears here (19:18), in the middle of the holiness laws.
- 1–4 · Moses looks back: forty years, from Horeb to the plains of Moab.
- 5–26 · The law retold: the Ten Commandments again, then how to live in the land.
- 27–30 · The covenant renewed: blessings and curses, ending with “choose life.”
- 31–34 · Moses’ last days: Joshua takes charge, then a song, a blessing and Moses’ death on Mount Nebo.
Speeches, not stories: most of the book is Moses talking to the new generation on the edge of the land, in the last days of his life.

The Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (6:4) is still said daily by Jews. Jesus calls the next verse the greatest commandment, and answers all three temptations in the wilderness with words from Deuteronomy.
The name: from the Greek for “second law,” the law given a second time.
- 1:1–3:6 · Two openings: the land left unconquered, then the pattern spelled out.
- 3:7–16:31 · Twelve judges: Othniel to Samson, each round a little worse than the last.
- 17–21 · Two closing stories: Micah’s idol and the Danites, then the crime at Gibeah and a civil war.
The cycle: Israel does evil, an enemy oppresses them, they cry out, the LORD raises up a judge, and the land has rest, until the judge dies and it starts again (2:11–19).
The downward spiral: the judges themselves get worse. Othniel is spotless, Gideon ends with an idol, Jephthah makes a terrible vow, and Samson breaks almost every vow he has.
“No king in Israel”: the closing chapters keep saying it (17:6, 18:1, 19:1, 21:25), and everyone does what is right in his own eyes. The book points ahead to the kings.
- 1 Chronicles 1–9 · Names: from Adam to the families who came home from exile, with the most room given to Judah, David’s tribe, and Levi, the temple tribe.
- 1 Chronicles 10–29 · David: the ark comes to Jerusalem, and David plans and gathers for the temple.
- 2 Chronicles 1–9 · Solomon: the temple is built and filled with glory.
- 2 Chronicles 10–36 · Judah’s kings: from the split to the exile, ending with Cyrus sending the people home.
Written for the returned: Chronicles retells Samuel and Kings for people back from Babylon, asking what the story means for them now. In Hebrew it is one book, and it comes last in the Hebrew Bible.
What it leaves out: the northern kings appear only when they touch Judah, and David’s sin with Bathsheba and Solomon’s fall aren’t told. The focus is the temple, worship and David’s line.

Seek the LORD: kings who seek the LORD prosper and kings who forsake him fall, often within the same reign. “If My people who are called by My name humble themselves and pray…” (2 Chronicles 7:14) sums it up.
“Also in”: stories told in Samuel or Kings too have a line under them that opens the other telling.
- 1 Chronicles 1–9 · Names: from Adam to the families who came home from exile, with the most room given to Judah, David’s tribe, and Levi, the temple tribe.
- 1 Chronicles 10–29 · David: the ark comes to Jerusalem, and David plans and gathers for the temple.
- 2 Chronicles 1–9 · Solomon: the temple is built and filled with glory.
- 2 Chronicles 10–36 · Judah’s kings: from the split to the exile, ending with Cyrus sending the people home.

What it leaves out: the northern kings appear only when they touch Judah, and David’s sin with Bathsheba and Solomon’s fall aren’t told. The focus is the temple, worship and David’s line.

“Also in”: stories told in Samuel or Kings too have a line under them that opens the other telling.
- 1–2 · The story opens: a blameless man loses everything, and three friends come to sit with him.
- 3–27 · The debate: three rounds of speeches, Job against Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar.
- 28–31 · A poem on wisdom, then Job’s last defense.
- 32–37 · Elihu: a younger man speaks up.
- 38–42 · The LORD answers from the whirlwind, and Job is restored.
Story around poetry: the opening and the close are told as a story. Everything in between is poetry.
The question underneath: does Job fear God “for nothing” (1:9)? The friends insist that suffering must mean sin. Job knows his doesn’t, and demands an answer.
No reason given: God never tells Job about the scene in heaven. He answers with the wonders of creation, and Job is satisfied.
Running out of words: the third round breaks down. Bildad’s last speech is six verses, and Zophar doesn’t speak at all.
- Book I (1–41) · Nearly all David. Mostly cries for help from a man under pressure, with trust breaking through.
- Book II (42–72) · The sons of Korah, then David again. Longing, confession and the king, closing with “the prayers of David son of Jesse are ended.”
- Book III (73–89) · Asaph and the sons of Korah. Hard questions: the temple in ruins, and in Psalm 89 the promise to David’s line seems broken.
- Book IV (90–106) · Opens with Moses. The answer to Book III: kings may fail, but the LORD reigns.
- Book V (107–150) · Gathered home. Thanks, pilgrim songs on the road to Jerusalem, and a rising flood of praise.
From cries to praise: cries for help crowd the first half of the book. Praise takes over toward the end, until the last five psalms are nothing but Hallelujah.
“God” or “the LORD”: in Psalms 42–83 the writers mostly say “God” (Elohim) where the rest of the book says “the LORD” (Yahweh). Psalm 53 even repeats Psalm 14 with the name changed.
Closing blessings: each of the five books ends with a short blessing of the LORD (41, 72, 89, 106), and Psalm 150 closes the whole book in praise. Many readers see an echo of the five books of Moses.
The big arc, as many readers see it: God’s King is crowned (2), the kingdom falls (89), the people learn again that the LORD reigns (93–100), and they come home singing (107–150).
- 1–9 · A father’s teaching: longer poems, with Wisdom and Folly calling out like two women in the street.
- 10:1–22:16 · Solomon’s proverbs: 375 two-line sayings, most setting the wise against the foolish.
- 22:17–24:34 · Sayings of the wise: thirty sayings, then a few more.
- 25–29 · More of Solomon’s proverbs, copied by King Hezekiah’s men.
- 30–31 · The words of Agur and of King Lemuel, ending with the noble wife.
The key: “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7).
Proverbs, not promises: each saying shows how life usually goes. Sometimes two sit side by side and seem to disagree (26:4–5), because being wise means knowing which one fits.
The last poem (31:10–31) is an acrostic: each verse starts with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet.
- 1–2 · The search: the Teacher tries wisdom, pleasure and hard work, and calls them all “futile.”
- 3–6 · Times and seasons: what lasts under the sun, and what doesn’t.
- 7–10 · What wisdom is worth, and where it runs out.
- 11–12 · Enjoy your days and remember your Creator before old age comes.
“Under the sun”: the phrase comes nearly 30 times. The Teacher looks at life from ground level, the way anyone can see it.
Futile: the Hebrew word means breath or vapor, something real but brief that slips through the fingers.
The conclusion: “Fear God and keep His commandments, because this is the whole duty of man” (12:13).
- 1:1–2:7 · Longing: the bride and her beloved find each other.
- 2:8–3:5 · Spring: he calls her to come away, and she searches for him at night.
- 3:6–5:1 · The wedding: Solomon’s procession and the bridegroom’s praise.
- 5:2–8:4 · Lost and found: a missed knock, a search through the city, and praise renewed.
- 8:5–14 · Love as strong as death.
Voices: the poem is sung by a woman, a man and a group of friends. Many Bibles mark who is speaking.
The refrain: “Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right” closes three of the sections (2:7, 3:5, 8:4).
How it has been read: as a celebration of love between husband and wife, and through the centuries also as a picture of God’s love for his people.
- 1–12 · Judah and Jerusalem: rebellion and judgment, Isaiah’s call, and the promise of Immanuel and a child to be born.
- 13–27 · The nations: messages against Babylon, Moab, Egypt, Tyre and more, then judgment on the whole earth.
- 28–35 · Woes and hope: don’t lean on Egypt; a king will reign in righteousness.
- 36–39 · History: Hezekiah, the Assyrian siege and the envoys from Babylon, also told in 2 Kings 18–20.
- 40–55 · Comfort: the LORD will bring his people home from Babylon, and his Servant will suffer for them.
- 56–66 · New creation: the nations stream to Zion, under new heavens and a new earth.
Two halves: chapters 1–39 mostly warn of judgment in Isaiah’s own day. Chapter 40 opens with “Comfort, comfort My people” and looks past the exile.
The Servant songs: four poems (42:1–9, 49:1–7, 50:4–11, 52:13–53:12) about the LORD’s Servant. The New Testament reads the last one as fulfilled in Jesus’ death.
“The Holy One of Israel”: Isaiah’s favorite name for God, used about 25 times across both halves.
- 1–25 · Warnings: Jeremiah’s call, sermons at the temple gate, and messages acted out with a linen belt, a potter’s clay and a broken jar.

- 26–45 · Jeremiah’s story: plots, prison and a muddy cistern, the scroll the king burns, the fall of Jerusalem and the flight to Egypt. In the middle, the Book of Comfort (30–33) promises a new covenant.
- 46–51 · Messages against the nations, from Egypt to Babylon.
- 52 · Jerusalem’s fall, told again as in 2 Kings 24–25.
Not in time order: the chapters jump between the reigns of Josiah, Jehoiakim and Zedekiah. Most chapters say which king it was.
The weeping prophet: Jeremiah tells God exactly how he feels. His complaints (11–20) are some of the rawest prayers in the Bible.
The new covenant: “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (31:33), quoted in full in Hebrews 8.
- 1 · The city weeps: Jerusalem as a widow with no one to comfort her.
- 2 · The Lord’s anger: what the siege did to the city.
- 3 · One man’s grief, with hope at the center: “His mercies never fail. They are new every morning” (3:22–23).
- 4 · Then and now: Zion’s people before the fall and after.
- 5 · A prayer: “Restore us to Yourself, O LORD.”

Acrostics: chapters 1, 2 and 4 have 22 verses each, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Chapter 3 gives every letter three verses, 66 in all. Chapter 5 has 22 verses but no alphabet, as if the pattern finally breaks.
Hope in the middle: the brightest words in the book sit at its exact center.
Grief in order: the alphabet holds the sorrow from first letter to last, mourning completely without being swallowed by it.
- 1–3 · The call: a vision of God’s glory by a river in Babylon.
- 4–24 · Judgment on Jerusalem: signs acted out, the glory leaving the temple, and the city’s sins laid bare.
- 25–32 · Messages against the nations, above all Tyre and Egypt.
- 33–39 · Hope after the fall: a good shepherd, a new heart, and dry bones that live again.
- 40–48 · A new temple: the glory returns, and a river flows out to bring life.

The glory moves: Ezekiel sees God’s glory leave the temple (10–11) before Jerusalem falls, and watches it come back to a new temple (43). The book’s last words name the city “THE LORD IS THERE” (48:35).
Acted-out messages: Ezekiel lies on his side for months, shaves his head and packs his bags for exile, turning his own life into the message.
“Then they will know that I am the LORD”: the line runs through the whole book, more than 50 times.
- 1–6 · Six court stories: Daniel and his friends stay faithful in Babylon, from the king’s food to the lions’ den.
- 7–12 · Four visions: beasts from the sea, a ram and a goat, seventy weeks, and the time of the end.
Two languages: from 2:4 to the end of chapter 7 the book is written in Aramaic, the language of the empire. The rest is Hebrew.
One message, twice: Nebuchadnezzar’s statue (2) and Daniel’s four beasts (7) both show four kingdoms giving way to a kingdom that will never end.
Even the kings say it: “His kingdom is an eternal kingdom” (4:3), from the mouth of Nebuchadnezzar.
- Before the exile · Hosea, Amos, Jonah and Micah, while Assyria was rising. Then Nahum, Habakkuk and Zephaniah, as Assyria fell and Babylon rose.
- Around the fall · Obadiah, most likely, against Edom for gloating when Jerusalem fell.
- After the exile · Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, among the people who came home.
- Joel · gives no date.
One scroll: in the Hebrew Bible these twelve short books are a single book, “The Twelve.” They’re called the Minor Prophets only because they’re short.
Hosea’s marriage: Hosea marries Gomer, who leaves him, and he buys her back (1–3). His broken marriage pictures God’s faithfulness to unfaithful Israel.
“The day of the LORD”: the phrase ties the Twelve together, from Joel and Amos to Malachi’s last chapter.
The last word: Malachi promises that Elijah will come before the great day (4:5). The Gospels open with John the Baptist.
- 1–4 · Beginnings: the son of David and son of Abraham, born in Bethlehem, baptized and tested.
- 5–25 · Five great talks, with stories between them: the Sermon on the Mount (5–7), sending out the Twelve (10), parables (13), life together (18), and the end of the age (24–25).
- 26–28 · The cross and the empty tomb, ending with “Go and make disciples of all nations.”
Five talks: each ends with nearly the same words, “When Jesus had finished…” (7:28, 11:1, 13:53, 19:1, 26:1). Many readers see an echo of the five books of Moses.
“To fulfill what was spoken”: Matthew quotes the prophets more than any other Gospel, showing Jesus as the one Israel was waiting for.
God with us: the book opens with Immanuel, “God with us” (1:23), and closes with “I am with you always” (28:20).
“Also in”: stories Mark tells too have a line under them that opens Mark’s telling.
- 1:1–8:26 · Galilee: one miracle after another, and the question “Who is this?”
- 8:27–10:52 · On the road: Peter says “You are the Christ,” and three times Jesus foretells his death.
- 11–16 · Jerusalem: one week, the cross and the empty tomb.
Fast: the shortest Gospel, often moving on “at once” or “immediately,” yet more than a third of it is spent on Jesus’ last week.
The hinge: Peter’s answer at Caesarea Philippi (8:29) is the middle of the book. Before it, people ask who Jesus is; after it, he teaches what kind of Christ he has come to be.
Keeping it quiet: Jesus often tells people not to say who he is, until a Roman centurion at the cross says it out loud: “Truly this man was the Son of God!” (15:39).
The ending: some of the earliest manuscripts stop at 16:8, with the women afraid at the empty tomb. Verses 9–20 are in most others.
- 1–2 · Two births: John and Jesus, told side by side, with songs from Mary, Zechariah and Simeon.
- 3:1–9:50 · Galilee: teaching, healing and calling disciples.
- 9:51–19:27 · The road to Jerusalem: ten chapters on the way, holding most of the parables only Luke tells.
- 19:28–24:53 · Jerusalem: the last week, the cross, and the risen Jesus on the road to Emmaus.
The turn: “Jesus resolutely set out for Jerusalem” (9:51). From there the whole story leans toward the city.
An orderly account: Luke tells Theophilus he has “carefully investigated everything from the beginning” (1:3). Acts is his second volume.
Who gets welcomed: shepherds, Samaritans, tax collectors, widows and a lost son. Luke keeps showing how far God’s welcome reaches.
“Also in”: stories Mark tells too have a line under them that opens Mark’s telling.
- 1:1–18 · The prologue: the Word who was with God and was God becomes flesh.
- 1:19–12:50 · The signs: seven signs, from water into wine to Lazarus raised, with long talks between them.
- 13–17 · The upper room: Jesus washes his friends’ feet and talks with them the night before he dies.
- 18–21 · The cross and the risen Jesus: Mary Magdalene, Thomas, and Peter restored by the sea.
Why it was written: “so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God” (20:31).

“I am”: seven sayings (the bread of life, the light of the world, the gate, the good shepherd, the resurrection and the life, the way and the truth and the life, the true vine) echo the name God gave Moses.
Its own telling: most of John isn’t in Matthew, Mark or Luke. There are no parables, and Jesus goes up to Jerusalem for several feasts.
- 1–7 · Jerusalem: the Spirit comes at Pentecost and the church grows, until Stephen is stoned.
- 8–12 · Judea and Samaria: Philip, Saul’s conversion, and Peter at the home of Cornelius, a Gentile.
- 13–20 · To the ends of the earth: Paul’s three journeys across Asia Minor and Greece.
- 21–28 · Paul on trial: arrested in Jerusalem, he appeals to Caesar and reaches Rome.
The outline in one verse: “you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem, and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (1:8).
Peter, then Paul: Peter leads the first half and Paul the second, and their stories mirror each other. Each heals a man who could not walk, and each is freed from prison.
“We”: from 16:10 the writer starts saying “we.” Luke himself traveled with Paul for parts of the journey.
- 1:1–17 · Greeting: Paul, who has never been to Rome, introduces the gospel he preaches.
- 1:18–3:20 · All have sinned: Gentiles and Jews alike stand guilty before God.
- 3:21–8:39 · Made right by faith: Abraham, Adam and Christ, freedom from sin and life in the Spirit, ending with nothing able to separate us from God’s love.
- 9–11 · Israel: has God’s word failed? Paul’s answer ends in praise.
- 12–16 · Living it out: living sacrifices, love, the strong and the weak, and greetings to friends.
The theme: the gospel “is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes” (1:16).
Built like an argument: Paul raises the objections himself (“What then shall we say?”) and answers them, as if a listener kept interrupting.
Written from Corinth, most likely around AD 57, before Paul’s visit to Rome.
- 1–4 · Better than angels and Moses: the Son is God’s final word.
- 5–10 · A better priest and sacrifice: Jesus, a high priest in the order of Melchizedek, brings a new covenant with one offering for all time.
- 11 · By faith: the long roll call, from Abel to the prophets.
- 12–13 · Run the race: endurance, discipline and a kingdom that can’t be shaken.
“Better”: the key word. Jesus is better than the angels, than Moses, than the priests and their sacrifices, and brings a better covenant with better promises.
Warnings woven in: five times the teaching stops to warn against drifting away (2:1–4, 3:7–4:13, 5:11–6:12, 10:19–39, 12:14–29).
No name given: the writer never says who he is. It reads like a sermon written down, and calls itself a “word of exhortation” (13:22).
- 1–3 · The risen Christ: John’s vision on Patmos and letters to seven churches.
- 4–5 · The throne room: worship in heaven, and the Lamb takes the scroll.
- 6–16 · Three sevens: seven seals, seven trumpets and seven bowls, with visions between them of a woman, a dragon and two beasts.
- 17–20 · The fall of Babylon, the rider on the white horse, and the final judgment.
- 21–22 · All things new: the new Jerusalem, where God lives with his people.
Sevens: seven churches, seals, trumpets and bowls. Seven runs through the book as the number of completeness.
Meant to be heard: “Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear” (1:3).
Echoes everywhere: it hardly ever quotes the Old Testament outright, yet hundreds of lines echo Daniel, Ezekiel, Isaiah, Exodus and the Psalms.
Garden to city: the Bible opens in a garden (Genesis 2) and closes in a city with a river and the tree of life (22:1–2).
